hanging-ghost.definition: 吊死鬼 / The Ghost Who Hanged Died by hanging due to poverty, grievance, or heartbreak (自缢身亡) Era of Death: Varies; most cases recorded in the Ming and Qing dynasties Current Ghostly Tier: Li Gui (厉鬼, Vengeful Spirit) Netherworld Jurisdiction: Under the Jurisdiction of the Ten Yama Kings, awaiting inevitable reclamation by the Netherworld Court
hanging-ghost.heroQA: The hanging rope still marks her throat, and the suffocation that killed her becomes the trap she sets for the living. She is not a ghost of malice—she is a ghost of memory, a soul caught in the final second of its own death, replaying that moment over and over, dragging others into it because she cannot bear to drown alone.
hanging-ghost.storyContext: Imagine the last thing you do before you die. For the Hanging Ghost, it was tying a knot. A simple, practical knot, the kind you use to secure a bundle of firewood or to hang a lantern. She tied it to a beam in her own home—the house where she raised her children, where she slept beside her husband for fifteen years. She stood on a stool. She put the rope around her neck. And she stepped off. In that last second, as the rope bit into her throat and the blood vessels in her eyes burst, she saw the ceiling of her own home, the one she had looked at a thousand times before, and she thought—she thought something. I don't know what. I don't think anyone does. Because that thought, whatever it was, never got to become a memory. It got cut off mid-sentence, just like her breath. And for the next thousand years, she has been repeating that last second over and over again, trying to finish the thought.
hanging-ghost.whyItMatters: You might have heard of the Hanging Ghost from Chinese horror films, from the stories your grandmother told you about the "old house at the end of the lane," or from the visual of a woman in white with a red rope around her neck, tongue extended, eyes wide. These stories are not wrong, exactly, but they miss the most important point. In the Western imagination, a ghost is usually a haunting anomaly—a ghost is something that *should not exist*, a bug in the system of reality, an unexplainable remnant of trauma. In Chinese cosmology, a ghost is not an anomaly. It is a defined, rule-governed intermediate state between death and reincarnation. The Hanging Ghost is not haunting a house because she is a broken record of trauma—she is there because the Netherworld Court has sentenced her to five hundred more years on that beam. She is there by cosmic law. Understanding her story means understanding that law, and that is what makes her story worth telling.

water-ghost.definition: 水鬼 / Shui Gui (Drowning Ghost) Drowned, the soul trapped at the bottom of the water, unable to leave (溺水而亡，魂魄困于水底，无法脱离) Era of Death: Not precisely recorded in any surviving chronicle; likely some time during the Ming or Qing dynasty, based on local folk accounts. Current Ghost Path Level: Li Gui (厉鬼, Vengeful Spirit) Underworld Jurisdiction: The local Water God's jurisdiction, with periodic patrol by the Ox-Head...
water-ghost.heroQA: Shui Gui (Water Ghost, the drowning spirit bound to the site of its own death) does not haunt the living out of malice. It haunts because the water will not let it leave, and because the only way to buy its own release is to pull another soul down into the same cold darkness.
water-ghost.storyContext: Imagine dying with your lungs full of water, and then not being allowed to leave. You don't go to heaven. You don't go to hell. You just stay at the bottom of the river, in the dark, your mouth still open, and every time someone walks by the shore, a part of your brain that is no longer fully human whispers: "If they come down here, I can go free." That's the Water Ghost—the Shui Gui. In the West, we have stories of drowned spirits luring people to their deaths, like the Lorelei or the rusalka. But the Chinese version adds a twist that is both more mechanical and more tragic: the drowned soul is a prisoner. It cannot leave the water, cannot cross over, until it finds a replacement. The ghost doesn't want to kill; it wants to escape. But the only key to the door is another person's death.
water-ghost.whyItMatters: You might have encountered the Water Ghost under different names—in old Chinese ghost stories, in a Zhang Yimou film, or in an urban legend your Chinese classmates told you about. It's one of the most common figures in Chinese folk ghostlore, as familiar as the Headless Horseman is in America. But the stories usually focus on the horror: the pale hand emerging from the reeds, the voice calling your name in the dark. What they don't tell you is the cosmic logic behind it. The Water Ghost is not a supernatural anomaly. It is a predictable symptom of how the Underworld handles souls that die in a specific way—a kind of bureaucratic glitch in the recycling system. To understand the Water Ghost is to understand, in a very concrete way, how the Chinese mythic universe treats the dead: not as souls who are automatically judged, but as souls who first have to get unstuck from the place where they died. Let's start from that moment of un-sticking, or the failure to un-stick.
